cases.abstract: Avoiding quadratic attention storage does not by itself keep a GPU busy: normalization arithmetic and poorly partitioned work can still limit exact attention. FlashAttention-2 reorganizes tiled attention around independently normalized query rows. Assigning these rows to separate warps removes forward inter-warp reductions, while distributing row blocks across thread blocks exposes parallelism when batches or head counts are small. Delaying output normalization reduces non-matrix arithmetic without approximating softmax or losing linear auxiliary memory. On an A100 80GB GPU, attention benchmarks with sequences of 512 to 16k tokens and 16k total tokens show 1.7-3.0-fold speedups over FlashAttention. For 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models trained on eight A100 GPUs at 2k or 8k context, gains reach 1.3-fold over FlashAttention, with peak reported throughput of 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU. Multi-query decoding has a different bottleneck: loading the key-value cache. Spreading these loads across thread blocks yields an attention-kernel speedup of up to sevenfold over FasterTransformer on A100. The training comparison shows that kernel acceleration delivers smaller, context-dependent whole-model gains.
cases.methods: Each query row has its own softmax denominator, so different rows can be assigned to different warps without splitting the calculation of a single output row. FlashAttention-2 uses this independence: every warp accesses the key and value tiles but produces only its assigned query rows. Unlike splitting keys among warps, this arrangement removes shared-memory reductions and synchronization from the forward output calculation. Query-row blocks also run independently across thread blocks, supplying parallel work when batch size and head count are too small to occupy the GPU. Within a row block, online softmax maintains the running maximum, exponential sum, and unnormalized weighted output. A changed maximum rescales accumulated quantities, but division by the sum occurs only after the final key tile, reducing non-matrix arithmetic while preserving exact attention. Rowwise log-sum-exp values support probability recomputation during backpropagation instead of quadratic storage; the backward pass still requires synchronization.
cases.results: Longer context makes the training benefit of faster attention more pronounced, but it does not turn a kernel speedup into an equal whole-model gain. On eight A100 80GB GPUs, replacing FlashAttention with FlashAttention-2 raises reported throughput for a 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, compared with 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B model reaches 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 8k, versus 175 with FlashAttention. These comparisons place the largest training gain near 1.3-fold, below the 1.7-3.0-fold attention-kernel gains in the separate A100 benchmarks. Those benchmarks also expose the storage constraint: standard PyTorch attention runs out of memory at 16k, whereas tiled implementations complete that setting. The reported peak 72% model FLOPs utilization counts causal attention using the conventional unhalved training formula. It should therefore be interpreted using that accounting convention, rather than as a direct count of executed arithmetic.
cases.notes: Connected row independence to work partitioning, then distinguished kernel acceleration from its context-dependent training payoff. Section 3 and Algorithm 1 support exactness and linear auxiliary memory; Section 4.1 supports the A100 kernel comparison; Table 1 supports training gains and the unhalved FLOPs convention; Figure 5 supports only multi-query attention-kernel decoding gains. The Results paragraph tests the end-to-end promise with the 2k/8k contrast and retains PyTorch's memory failure. Applied the guide's bottleneck-to-measurement transfer without attributing isolated speed contributions to individual changes or treating future hardware optimizations as completed results.

cases.abstract: Autoregressive generation can leave computational capacity unused while a large model waits for each preceding token. Speculative decoding uses that capacity to verify a cheaper model's proposed continuation in parallel, without requiring the draft to reproduce the target's probabilities. An acceptance rule preserves the probability mass shared by the models, and a residual distribution corrects rejected proposals, yielding exactly the target sampling distribution for any draft model without retraining the target. The analysis connects latency to the balance between acceptance and proposal cost, assuming independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and concurrent verification that takes no longer than one target step. In batch-one tests on a single TPU-v4 against T5X decoding, a 77M-parameter T5-small draft accelerates 11B-parameter T5-XXL by 2.6-fold on English-German translation and 2.3-fold on summarization under standard sampling. Greedy decoding reaches 3.4-fold and 3.1-fold, respectively. Larger draft models achieve higher acceptance but lower walltime gains, showing that improved agreement must compensate for proposal cost. These gains exploit concurrency rather than fewer arithmetic operations and require spare computational resources.
cases.methods: Let p and q denote target and draft token distributions after sampling adjustments. A token x drawn from q is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); after rejection, a replacement is drawn from the normalized positive part of p - q. Acceptance supplies mass min(p(x), q(x)), and the correction supplies the missing target mass, so the combined distribution is exactly p. Parallel verification evaluates every draft prefix, but only the proposals preceding the first rejection are retained. Correction at that prefix, or an extra target token if all proposals pass, guarantees at least one output per iteration. For gamma proposals and mean acceptance alpha, independent, identically distributed acceptance rates give an expected yield of (1 - alpha^(gamma + 1))/(1 - alpha). Dividing this yield by 1 + gamma*c predicts walltime speedup for sufficiently long outputs if concurrent verification costs one target step; c is the draft-to-target step-time ratio.
cases.results: The T5 comparisons show why the draft with the highest acceptance need not minimize latency. On a single TPU-v4 at batch size one, greedy English-German translation with an 11B-parameter T5-XXL target and a T5-small draft achieves 3.4-fold speedup over T5X decoding at an acceptance rate of 0.75. With the same seven-token proposal length, T5-large increases acceptance to 0.82 but yields only 1.7-fold speedup. Greater agreement therefore does not by itself offset a more expensive proposal model. T5-small also illustrates the sampling dependence: translation acceptance falls to 0.62 under standard sampling, and speedup falls to 2.6-fold; summarization speedup likewise falls from 3.1-fold to 2.3-fold. These measured latency gains are specific to the implemented T5 experiments; GPT-like and LaMDA tests report acceptance rather than walltime. Rejection discards already evaluated continuations, so the method can consume more arithmetic work even while finishing sooner on hardware with spare compute.
cases.notes: Explained why distributional disagreement is compatible with exact sampling, then used draft-size comparisons to test the acceptance-cost tradeoff. Section 2.3 supplies the correction rule; Sections 3.1-3.3 supply the conditional yield and walltime analysis; Table 2 supplies batch-one TPU-v4 latency comparisons against T5X. Table 3 supplies acceptance measurements only for GPT-like and LaMDA models. Applied the guide's equivalence-enabling-operation transfer in Methods, not its external claims. Distribution preservation does not require the performance assumptions. Larger drafts and extra arithmetic remain consequential adverse findings; oracle-based adaptation remains unimplemented.
